messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Function documentation in the manual; feedback requested
parts:
Hi all,

Here are some options for the documentation. It's on the feature/issue-843-test-nan-Phi branch, if you want to edit manually.

I've put together 3 options.
1. the main use first, infinite cases not explicitly mentioned.
2. ordered by range of x, inf explicitly mentioned
3. every case broken out, including inf, nan.

Other thoughts:
- should we use a different notation for ranges?
- Phi(x) on the left side -- should it be in the code font?
- location of the definition of \Phi(x)? use of \equiv?

On Friday, August 22, 2014 10:01:20 AM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
Here are some options for the documentation. It's on the feature/issue-843-test-nan-Phi branch, if you want to edit manually.

I've put together 3 options.
1. the main use first, infinite cases not explicitly mentioned.
Yes

Other thoughts:
- should we use a different notation for ranges?
I think this is fine. If you thinking about the alternative notation, $x \in \left(-37.5,8.25\right)$, that can be confusing in some countries.
- Phi(x) on the left side -- should it be in the code font?
Yeah, I think that would emphasize that Phi(x) is the computational implementation and $\Phi\left(x\right)$ is the mathematical function.
- location of the definition of \Phi(x)? use of \equiv?

Nah, if we are emphasizing that Phi(x) is the computational implementation, then $\equiv$ would seem counter to that.

Ben

P.S. We also need to implement Phi_inv(p) soon, such that Phi_inv(Phi(x)) = x. But should Phi_inv(0) return -37.5 + epsilon or -inf? I guess input to Phi_inv() that was less than 0 or greater than 1 would throw an exception nowdays, rather than NaN or an infinite value.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: inverse cdf behavior at 1 and 0
parts:
[change subject]

more below
> On Aug 22, 2014 11:08 AM, "Ben Goodrich" <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > P.S. We also need to implement Phi_inv(p) soon, such that Phi_inv(Phi(x)) = x. But should Phi_inv(0) return -37.5 + epsilon or -inf? I guess input to Phi_inv() that was less than 0 or greater than 1 would throw an exception nowdays, rather than NaN or an infinite value.

I'm not sure what inv_Phi(0) or inv_Phi(1) should do. On the
one hand, I'm tempted to go with the behavior of log and exp,
with Phi(-inf) = 0, inv_Phi(0) = -inf, and similarly for +inf and 1.
On the other, that's going to be an automatic rejection. What
do the gradients look like out at the edges?

I believe we've been somewhat inconsistent about this in that
I think we make sure inv_logit doesn't underflow to 0 or overflow to
1 no matter what the input. I'm not sure that's right either.

There's no way to make the thing properly invertible outside
of (-38,38) or thereabouts (if that's where things overflow or
underflow with double).

- Bob

No, it should be in math.

> 4. Space between groups is 6pt. Look about right?

Yes, \infty please. This follows from the whole thing being math.

For distributions, I was using \mbox{\sf Poisson}, which I
commonly see in books. That's a bit different than \mbox{\tt Poisson}
or \code{Poisson}, which renders in "typewriter" code font.
> Also, should we keep this group if it's obvious from the first group? I would think x = inf is included in x > 8.25, but I'm happy to include it for consistency.

I was about to say that. When it follows from comparisons, no
reason to include it. I'm OK including it if we want to be
super specific -- that way the functions would match that aren't
defined with conditionals.

Are you going to define exp() the same way, with

exp(x) = e^x if x \in [-800,800]
= 0 if x < -800
= inf if x > 800

or whatever the bound is?

This might be useful to our users to give them ideas of the scales at
which arithmetic is even remotely feasible.
> 6. I'm separating out NaN as its own group. I tried putting it within the same group as inf and it looked a little odd, but could be convinced to go that way.

> 7. "throws exception"? Is that clear enough? Not all functions throw; some return NaN, others return booleans or integers, so it'll probably be worth documenting behavior for each function for NaN. For the infinity cases, I could see us not explicitly stating what happens on the bounds if it's obvious. For Phi, if x = inf case isn't written out, I think it's still clear.

I'm ok with just "error" or "exception". It might be even better just
to say on the outside that NaN raises an exception --- it doesn't
return the value "throw exception" as the equality sign seems to imply now
that I look at it.
> 8. between ":" and "x" I've added a large space ("\;"). Does that look ok?

I prefer \mbox{if }. With a single trailing space.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Function documentation in the manual; feedback requested
parts:
I think you’re trying to do too much with too few elements.  There are four key pieces that you’re trying to present:

1) The function signature
2) The function description in words
3) The mathematical definition
4) The implementation

At the very least I think you should have something like

signature (as is)
Description (as is once you remove the equation)
Mathematical definition displayed on new line
Implementation (as is)

But I disagree on the level of implementation detail.  The user shouldn’t need to know when we transition from
erf to 0 or 1, it should just work.  What is useful to the user is not the implementation but rather

1) the mathematical domain of the function
2) the practical domain of the function

(2) is the only part of the implementation that is useful to the user.  For Phi it’s all double values, but for exp
we’re limited to log(max_double) and for something like phi_inv we can quote the threshold values where
everything becomes indistinguishable from the boundary.

So, for example,

\code{ real exp(real x) }
    The natural exponential function
        exp(x) = e^{x}

    Domain: -infty < x < infty
    Range: 0 < exp(x) < infty
    
    Implementation Domain: -max_double < x < log(max_double)
    Range: 0 < exp(x) < max_double

Lastly, if boundary values are really considered important then we should include a plot of the function
as that will be far more informative anyways.

> I think you’re trying to do too much with too few elements.

> 4) The implementation
Good breakdown.

> At the very least I think you should have something like

> Mathematical definition displayed on new line

I take it from the example you mean like you'd find it in
Wikipedia or in an algebra book?

> Implementation (as is)
>
> But I disagree on the level of implementation detail. The user shouldn’t need to know when we transition from
> erf to 0 or 1, it should just work.

I'm not sure what you mean here. It's only going to work as
far as floating point and our implementation let it.

> What is useful to the user is not the implementation but rather
>
> 1) the mathematical domain of the function
> 2) the practical domain of the function

I agree that they don't need to know about and should not be told
about implementation details. So they don't need to know when
log1p(x) transfers from the built-in definition to a Taylor series
at first or second order.

I also agree that the practical domain's what's important.

>
> (2) is the only part of the implementation that is useful to the user. For Phi it’s all double values, but for exp
> we’re limited to log(max_double) and for something like phi_inv we can quote the threshold values where
> everything becomes indistinguishable from the boundary.
>
> So, for example,
>
> \code{ real exp(real x) }
> The natural exponential function
> exp(x) = e^{x}
>
> Domain: -infty < x < infty
> Range: 0 < exp(x) < infty
>
> Implementation Domain: -max_double < x < log(max_double)

This brings up the issue of how to code this.

What you have is the implementation domain that'll produce
a finite result.

If you extend the implementation domain above log(max_double)
you get +inf. That includes +inf itself.

This to me seems the same kind of issue as underflowing to 0.


> Range: 0 < exp(x) < max_double

This is the finite range of output, but the full range will also
include +inf and NaN. But it can't produce negative numbers
or -inf.

> Lastly, if boundary values are really considered important then we should include a plot of the function
> as that will be far more informative anyways.

That would be great. I think most things
would benefit from both a linear and log-scale
plot. But that's probably asking too much to do in
this pass.

- Bob

messages.author: 6ad178c9bfa534b7
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Function documentation in the manual; feedback requested
parts: Is there a way to make the function signatures in the manual more machine readable? Right now for stan-mode and the pygments lexer, I have a json file with function signatures and documentation: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan-mode/blob/master/stan_lang.json.  However, I generate in an embarrassingly manual way from a text file https://github.com/stan-dev/stan-mode/blob/master/scripts/stan-reference.txt based on the output of pdftotext of the pdf version of the manual that has been manually edited.  I use this file to generate lists of functions and snippets.  I had tried to find a good parser for LaTeX but never had much luck.   I don't have a great suggestion; using templates to generate the manual adds another dependency and complications.
On Fri, Aug 22, 2014 at 7:01 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

Hi all,

Here are some options for the documentation. It's on the feature/issue-843-test-nan-Phi branch, if you want to edit manually.

1. the main use first, infinite cases not explicitly mentioned.

3. every case broken out, including inf, nan.

Other thoughts:
- should we use a different notation for ranges?
- Phi(x) on the left side -- should it be in the code font?
- location of the definition of \Phi(x)? use of \equiv?

This handles everything but the operators.
